image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |

4. Friends For Sale?

1. I notice that there is a left skew for people making friends in college and a right skew for the ones who make friends in the neighborhood. For making friends in high school and at work, the graphs are uniform. I also notice that people with a lower income make 1.9x more friends than average and people with higher incomes are 2.4x more likely to make friends than average. 

2. I wonder if the reason that people with a lower income are more likely than average to make friends in the neighborhood be because they help each other out to get through life and form a stronger bond between each other. For the higher income people, I wonder if the more money they have, means the more they will be able to do. So, they will be able to meet more people or do more and make more friends. 

3. This relates to me and my community because as a high school student, it is nice to see that income is not a big deal. For the most part, everyone makes around the same amount of friends. Also, in my neighborhood, it isn't rare to see people being friendly with each other and make friends. Since most neighborhoods seem to have their own specific groups, it is easier for them to relate to each other in certain circumstances which allows them to become friends easily. 

4. Do Income Levels Affect Where Friendships Start?

1) Depending on your income, you may have a better chance of meeting friends where you go to school, work, or reside. I noticed that the "high school" and "at work" graphs are nearly symmetric, with little variation due to income, implying that income has little impact on the forging of friendships. However, in college, those with higher incomes are 2.4x more likely to make friends, as shown by a left skew, but in the neighborhood, people with lower incomes are 1.9x more likely to make friends, as indicated by a right skew.

2) I'm curious whether altering the age category of this poll would significantly impact the findings or if they will remain the same. I'm curious why people with higher incomes are more likely to make friends at college whereas people with lower incomes are more likely to make friends in their communities.

3) Because I live in a small town, everyone's wage is nearly the same, which allows for greater contact in neighborhoods and at school. My high school has little to no income disparity, therefore while not being in the age range for which the graphs were created, I can relate to the high school situation shown here. However, I can imagine a college setting with students from all over the country adding to the income difference, forming parties based on wealth rather than real connections.

4) Are Your Friendships as Sound as a Dollar?

Is the difference still statistically significant though?

3) My school is a well-funded school serving disproportionately higher-income families, so it is likely that many in my community will gain more friends in college than from their neighborhoods.

4) More Money, Different Friends?

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.

     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |

3. Neighbourhoods around me show a similar pattern as displayed in the "In the neighbourhood" graph. For example, neighbourhoods with more concentrations of high-income demographics tend to engage less with community activities, festivals or gatherings.

1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |
raw_comment:
What do you notice? I notice that graphs for in high school and at work have a similar shape and have a peak near the center, indicating that most friends were made among people with a middle/average income. Meanwhile, the graphs for college and in the neighborhood are polar opposites. Most people making friends in college are those of higher income and it is 2.4 times more likely than the average. Most people making friends in the neighborhood are those that lower come and it is 1.9 times more likely than the average.

What do you wonder? I wonder why as a society we are allowing income to determine the relationships or friendships that are made. I wonder if it has to do with the different opportunities that rise in college and neighborhoods, given that there is less of a common goal. Schools have a main goal of graduating and in a working environment to get a paycheck. Meanwhile most people have a different goal in college and neighborhoods.

How does this relate to me and my community? This relates to me because I am a senior in high school so I relate to the high school graph. From my personal experience, I have made friends and will continue to make friends with people of all income levels. I have noticed most if not all my peers do the same when it comes to making friends. I think a lot of this has to do with the fact that we all share similar incomes.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the reason high school may be so small is because the audience answering the question is between the ages of 25 and 44. Memory deteriorates over time, and it would make sense that in this case, the high school experience would be forgotten. However, it makes me think of how brief high school is and how friends wait in other places.
I inferred that college friends come from money. If one is barely scraping by and is using in their resources to arrive at the highest potential, they will study and attend classes, focusing. Americans who have enough money will be more likely to attend secondary institutes. No one in college has enough money, but there is an abundance of friends.
As far as work friends go, they seem to come from where one falls in the workplace food chain. If you are in manual labor, you won’t be talking to those in ranks above you, and if you are a director or coordinator, you won’t be stopping by everyone’s offices checking in. I can assume that, if the graph went further, the symmetry would not change, rather, it could follow the trend. 
And finally, in the neighborhood, those who don’t have much in the material sense have the most in companionship. Those who live so close to each other, are usually roughly in the same boat, and have nothing to prove to those around them, making more friends in the long run.

If I were to name this graph, I would have it titled something along the lines of “Proof That Friends Are More Important Than Money”.

4) What’s going on in this graph?
My title would be "Does Money Buy Friends?"

raw_comment:
In high school, I see that people generally make friends no matter their income. In college, people make an exponentially higher amount of friends, almost 2.5 times the average, when they have a higher income. I am curious whether this is because having a job in college exposes people to more opportunities to make friends. In neighborhoods, people who make less money make more friends. The lowest level of income has more than twice the average number of friends. In the workplace, more friends are likely with average pay than a higher or lower income. 
I wonder mostly why income is being compared to friends and if the two are realistically related. I am also curious if people make more friends in their neighborhood when they have a lower income because they have more time for socialization. I also wonder how income was compared in high school students and if people who make no money are considered. 
This graph relates to me because as a high school student, it makes sense that people of all incomes make friends. People are not judged based on whether they have a job or not. 
A title for this graph would be "What does it cost to make a friend?"

| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that for high school students, income has no effect on making friends as both sides have x0.9, meaning it should be equal. On the other hand, I noticed that the other graphs aren’t equal at all. The graph for college students is skewed to the left, meaning that on average, people with higher income are more likely to befriend each other in college than those with less income. It’s the opposite for the graph showing the neighborhood as it has a right skew instead meaning those with lower incomes in neighborhoods are more likely to befriend each other than those with higher incomes.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why there are such differences between the graphs and why the community people are in plays such a big role in whether people with certain incomes make friends or not. I also wonder if it’s a coincidence that people with higher incomes make more friends at college and people with lower incomes make more friends in a neighborhood and if there may be a third variable at play.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because at school it really feels like anyone could become friends regardless of their income. It may be because money isn’t so important at this age, but I think the data is correct in saying those with lower incomes and those with higher incomes are equally likely to make friends in high school.

Headline
Where Wealthy Friendships are Wealthily Found: Make Friends by Income Rank

raw_comment:
I noticed the “In high school” and “At work” income levels followed the same pattern with a roughly normal, symmetrical shape. The “In college” and “In the neighborhood” were skewed left and right respectively. 

I wonder whether the number of friends people have also depends on income. The graphs show the percentage of where the friends were made, but that might be better understood in light of how many friends those with different incomes have. 

This relates to me because I am about to start the next phase of my life in college and it is interesting to know the chances of making friends in college or in a neighborhood setting. It is relevant to my community because where friends are made is heavily tied to current issues like accessibility, transportation, and available time outside of work and school.

In the graphs, the “In high school” section shows that most people make an average number of friends in high school, regardless of income. In “At work,” this difference is more pronounced, with the middle-income percentile making the highest percentage of friends in the workplace. In the “In college” graph, it is clear that those with a higher income make a larger percentage of their friends in college. Those with a lower income make a higher percentage of their friends “In the neighborhood” than other social places. One potential headline could be “The Real Fortune: Friends and Finances”.

The graph represents the likelihood of people to make friends in different locations depending on their income. The blue portions of the bars represent those who make more friends than average in that location.

I wonder how the answers would have changed if they were to poll a larger age demographic than just people between the ages of 25 to 44.

I observe that across all of the income levels people tend to make friends in high school. The is likely because high school is a universal experience, relatively independent of income. The upper wealth classes (60th-100th) are well above average in making friends in college. This is due to the fact that college is very expensive, meaning that it would be the foremost place for wealthy people to make friends. The opposite is true for the neighborhood. Those in the lowest income levels report making the most friends in this location.

This relates to me and my community in the sense that I am currently in high school, where friendship is equal across income levels. However, it is necessary to understand the ways that income can affect all areas of our lives. Through analyzing this graph we can gain insights into our society, such as the inaccessibility of college for lower income levels.

Friendship According to Income: Can Money Truly Buy Friends?

raw_comment: I notice that for students in high school, income rank does not play a huge role in making friends because the graph is uniform. There is a slight increase around the middle 50% of income and slight dips at both extremes. This is similar to the graph of those making friends at work. This could be because people in high schools don't necessarily care much about their classmates' income, and they make friends with them based on who they are instead of how much they make. Similarly, it is possible that those that work together may not care as much about how much their colleague makes because they all work in the same environment. I also notice that income plays a role in making friends in college and neighborhoods. In college, people who. make a higher income are 2.4x more likely to make friends, while in the neighborhood, it's the reverse; people who make a lower income are 1.9x as likely to make friends. I wonder why this is. Is it because people in college want to go on experiences and trips, so they become friends with people who make more money? Do people with a lower income make friends in neighborhoods because they come across as more relatable and less intimidating or snobbish? This relates to me because I don't consider income to be a main factor in making friends, but it makes me wonder if people around me do. My headline is "Rags or Riches: How income plays a role in making friends."

raw_comment: High income people are much more likely to make friends in college, while low income people are much more likely to make friends in their community. People of all incomes seem fairly equally likely to make friends in high school, as well as the likelihood of making friends at work being fairly distributed, with it being somewhat more likely for middle-income people. I wonder why friendships from high school are so evenly distributed. Maybe it's because of our country's system of free education through 12th grade, while the reason richer people are more likely to have friends from college is because they're more likely to be able to afford going to college at all. Though that begs the question of why are rich people so much less likely to make friends in their communities? They have houses. They have neighborhoods. Do higher income people spend too much time with work to participate in community socialization? No, because if that were the case, rich people should be more likely to have friends from work, which they aren't. Strange. I wonder about the reasons for these differences in friendships because I'm not sure what income my future will lead me to. Will a certain path cause me to develop friendships with certain people less easily? The graph doesn't make clear why, but it looks likely that if I manage to become wealthy, I may not have a good relationship with my community members.    A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |

raw_comment: What I take from this graph is that the proportion of friends made from high school or work settings is approximately equal between lower and higher incomes. This makes sense because almost the entire population would be engaged in high school and work environments. However, when it comes to college, there is a strong correlation between higher income and friends made in college; this makes sense because generally, careers stemming from a college education have higher incomes, and therefore those with higher incomes would have likely gone to college, and consequently made more friends in college. When it comes to neighborhoods, there is a strong correlation between lower incomes and making friends. This also makes sense because those who have higher incomes are less likely to live in communal neighborhoods, and therefore are less likely to make friends within a neighborhood. This graph is, as a gestalt, commenting on the fact that everyone makes friends in their own group, more likely or unlikely based on the fact that lower incomes are correlated with neighborhood living, and higher incomes are correlated with college and higher education. I would name this graph “Everyone Has Friends Somewhere”

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that in high school, the amount of friends one may have tends to stay the same regardless of their income. However, in college there seems to be a connection between income and the amount of friends one has. There is a 2.4% increase when it comes to having more friends as long as their income also increases. Similarly to the increase, there is a 0.3% decrease in friends for those who have a smaller source of income. At work, making friends is similar to that of highschool with only the tiniest difference of income. While there is this difference, it does not have a significant impact on making friends. Alongside this, the bar representing those who make friends in their neighborhood seems to be skewed to the right as the likelihood of making friends is opposite to that of college.

2) I wonder why people let income influence whether they want to have friends or not. Why is it that friends come and go based directly on income in college? I also wonder what these graphs might look like in other countries where there are more influences. 

3) This relates to me and my community since we come from a pretty low-income area. Our town isn't as big either, which allows so many of us to start off with friends that may follow us into college since we've grown up with them. As a soon to be senior, I may see the difference once I enter college as students may only want to be friends with those of higher wealth classes.

4) "There's Been an Influx: in Friends or Income?"

   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

raw_comment:
I notice that the graph related to high school is symmetrical, meaning there is little correlation between income and making friends in that area, while in college, there is a right skew showing that high-income people are far more likely to gain friends in college, while in the neighborhood, there is a left skew showing the opposite in that area. This shows that those who are richer tend to make friends in areas where strangers may be present, and lower-income people tend to make more friends in areas where people are closer and more familiar. 

I wonder why something like having money can lead to having significantly higher rates of meeting friends in college, but not in the workplace or in high school, which are somewhat similar environments. I wonder what aspect of the neighborhood makes rich people unable to meet friends in that area, to such a low degree. 

In a lower income area, we tend to basically never see people in the higher income category, so being able to relate or make friends with people like that in our area would be nearly impossible, and as I am about to enter college as a high school senior, I may notice it more difficult to find friends when the more wealthy statically have an advantage over me in that department.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |
raw_comment:
1. It seems as though income disparity shines most brightly in places where not all tax brackets will be represented equally. Take the college graph, the clearest indicator of a correlation between wealth and the ability to make friends. First and foremost, lower-income families and children from those families don't have access to college, but that's relatively clear and obvious. What isn't so obvious is the fact that those few low-income children who do have the chance to go to college might a. have to work a job in order to pay their tuition or b. they're hyper-aware of the opportunity college presents and they want to make the best of it. 

2. What questions is this supposed to raise? We know there's a huge educational schism between the wealthy and the poor, so what can be done to not only bridge the gap educationally but also make the experiences of those low-income students more beneficial from a social standpoint.

3.  I'm fortunate enough to go to a really fantastic school with incredible people and teachers surrounding me every day, but I've never taken any time to consider the effects that come from a different socioeconomic class that the majority of students in the school come from might mean socially. I understand that the data references both high school and college, but I'm curious to see if there's a divide in that high school data between public and private high schools. 

4. A Friendly Investment: The Cost of Friendship

What do you notice?
I've seen that there are different links between friends and income; the lower your income, the more friends you make, and high school has the fewest friends made.

What do you wonder?
I'm curious why those with lower wages are less likely to establish acquaintances at work. I would assume that people who work earn more money and make more friends than those who live in their neighborhood. I also wonder why folks in their neighborhood earn so much less than everyone else.

How does this relate to you and your community?
The influence this has on my community and myself is that it will inform me how many friends I will make in various aspects of my life, as well as how much money I and they will make. People in our community have friends from our neighborhood and high school, and despite the fact that most of us go to college, our entire family resides in town, so we are always connected and return to town.

What’s going on in this graph?
"Can Money Bring Connection?"

1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |

2. image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |
